title: Orchids

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Botanists recognise between 21,950 and 26,049 species of orchids, and discover some 250 new species every year. Orchids live in every habitat on Earth except glaciers, which is not to say they cannot tolerate cold – they have been seen to grow north of the Arctic Circle and on some sub-Antarctic islands – but the tropics are where they have evolved most spectacularly. Orchids are considered the most advanced and diverse flowering family. Like the Detroit car manufacturers of the 1960s and their vehicles, evolution has added embellishments and adornments to orchids that appear to serve no purpose except the expression of beauty and style.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: After insects evolved winged flight around 330 million years ago, flowers everywhere have used them to carry pollen between males and females in order to continue their species. Nonetheless, the way in which some orchids do this has long been a source of debate. The orchid Bulbophyllum nocturnum was only recently discovered on a remote island in Papua New Guinea. Bulbophyllum nocturnum is the only orchid known to flower solely in darkness, and only over a single night – researchers could not comprehend what insect it could hope to attract for such a limited period. Nor had they seen before such strange-looking extensions to the petals, that resembled small sausages. But then they realised that they looked just like slime mould, the favourite food of night-flying tropical midges – an insect common on the island.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Indeed, orchids frequently surprise botanists. In New Zealand, Corybas carsei is perhaps one of the rarest orchids, known to live in only a single location. It was presumed extinct until the 1980s, when it was rediscovered through pure good luck by a team surveying a wetland for another purpose. This was a massive moment for orchid science, partly because this species was discovered to be different from an Australian species it had previously been classified with, but also because so many Corybas carsei specimens were discovered at that time. But when scientists returned to the area a decade later, Corybas carsei had vanished once more. They continued their research and discovered that in the old days, sparks from passing steam trains would frequently set fire to this whole wetland. So to the astonishment of some observers, the scientists started lighting small fires. And they came to understand that periodic fires weren't just a part of wetland life, they were essential to the survival of the orchid. In 2008, a search found 79 Corybas carsei in the wetland and in 2011 more than 200 were counted.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Another recent discovery was originally thought to be the orchid Tarniopbyllum norfolkianum. This is an 'epiphyte' - meaning a plant that grows on another plant – and has been found only in one place in New Zealand. Orchid expert Peter de Lange suspects that, in fact, it isn't Tarniopbyllum norfolkianum at all, but a completely new orchid species. What's more, to the astonishment of his team, it's been found living only on gorse, a species of hardy shrub introduced to New Zealand from Europe. De Lange believes this is important because, for decades, work to protect the environment in New Zealand has focussed on destroying all such introduced species in order to protect native flora. But if the orchid is eventually recognised as a new species that lives on gorse, it will suggest that this policy has been misguided. Uncertainty about the New Zealand orchid's true identity highlights another critical issue: scientists need to learn a lot more about the species that live there.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: It isn't for lack of interest, however. The Nodding Greenhood orchid, Pterastylis nutans, was first discovered in New Zealand in 1914 by collector Henry Matthews. He filled tray after tray of specimens for a museum until sometime around 1920, when he'd collected Pterostylis nutans to local extinction in northern New Zealand, although a few specimens survived further south. Such extreme behaviour is not uncommon in relation to orchids. Nineteenth-century European collectors sometimes suffered from a form of 'orchid madness'. Collectors journeyed to every corner of the globe for new acquisitions, and would sometimes lie regarding their destinations to confuse their rivals, because new specimens could be sold for ridiculous prices in London auction houses. And perhaps little has changed. In 2004 two seemingly respectable visiting scientists were arrested trying to illegally smuggle native orchids out of New Zealand. They had more than 100 plants, and for several weeks had been under observation by the Wildlife Enforcement Group.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Meanwhile, the work of reputable scientists continues. In the national museum, researcher Carlos Lehnebach preserves the first ever orchid samples collected in New Zealand by the Swedish naturalist Daniel Solander in 1769. Some of the tiny flowers are now just brown granules, but a few other specimens still exhibit the faintest hint of colour. Lehnebach is so fascinated by his subject that he's moved from his native Chile to investigate the Spider Orchid, Nematoceras trilobum. So far he's managed to locate it clustered around the entrances of caves, and now he's investigating the insect believed to be responsible for pollination. It's just one more example of the passion people feel for orchids.
